prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest combination of originality, demonstrated impact and unambiguous credit on the shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between many atoms and Doppler/recoil-free interrogation, and Ye's group then drove the Sr clock to uncertainties near 1e-18 and showed that many-body physics in the lattice is a resource and a systematic to be controlled. The result is already used for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and searches for dark-sector physics, and it has been reproduced in many laboratories over two decades, with a redefinition of the second under serious discussion. The two-name configuration matches the supplied credit exactly. I ranked it eighth in my opening ballot, which I now regard as too low: that placement reflected my own field's pull and a worry about overlap with earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes, not a scientific weakness of the candidate. Four colleagues placed it first and two second, and their attribution and maturity arguments are consistent and convincing.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the second has not yet been redefined, so the practical flagship application is still prospective, and that the idea sits in a lineage already recognised in 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (control of single trapped ions). Credit also reaches beyond the supplied pair: Sr and Yb lattice work at other laboratories (for example Takamoto and others, and the national metrology institutes) and ion-clock groups made comparable contributions. Ye is also credited under other candidate lines, which could matter for balance. These are real qualifications, but none removes the central point that Katori's concept and Ye's performance records define the achievement.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B004) are exactly an advance in what we can measure: magic-wavelength trapping with ultranarrow transitions reaching about 1e-18, with a clean Katori and Ye attribution.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and maturity and have moved my view accordingly. I would qualify one point: Kroll treats the missing names (Takamoto, Sr-lattice colleagues) as a footnote, whereas I think the citation should be worded around the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 1e-18 rather than around timekeeping in general, so that it does not implicitly claim credit for the whole optical-clock field. If a redefinition of the second has not occurred, we should avoid wording that depends on it.

responses.point: IceCube (B032) opened a new observational window, with a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and evidence for TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, and a discovery of this kind rewrites what astrophysics can observe.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously and I do not equate B004's broader support with greater merit. My reservation is attribution rather than science: a detector with hundreds of collaborators, AMANDA predecessors and a three-name limit make the choice of Halzen, Karle and Yoshida a judgement that Danielsson himself says rests on unverified background knowledge. The source associations are also still at moderate significance. For that reason I place B032 below B004 for this year, though I would not object to revisiting it once source evidence firms up.

responses.point: B004 is first, with IceCube second and Cirac and Zoller third; Pearce notes that Wineland's earlier recognition weakens the case for double recognition of trapped-ion work.
responses.response: I agree that the 2012 prize weakens B023 as an experimental-realisation story, and that is the main reason I no longer lead with Cirac and Zoller although I ranked them second. The 1995 gate proposal and the cold-atom simulation theory are original, but a theory-only prize adjacent to 2012 needs a stronger case than a metrology achievement with no comparable precedent for lattices. I keep B023 as my first alternative rather than my preferred choice.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B016 second and warns that overlap between the Hubbard-simulation candidate and Cirac and Zoller risks an unfair partitioning of credit.
responses.response: That partition concern is the right one and is one reason I would not combine B023 with another atoms-and-lattices part: Zoller and Cirac appear in both B016 and B023, and the three-person limit would force a choice that I cannot justify scientifically. It supports keeping B004, which has no such overlap, as the preferred single-achievement prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Cirac and Zoller sixth and Circuit QED seventh, citing the closeness of both to prior prizes in quantum control (2012) and superconducting circuits (2025).
responses.response: I partly agree. On circuit QED the proximity to 2025 is a genuine concern, and I raised it myself in my opening ballot; I would add that the credit problem (four credited names, three seats, Blais the obvious casualty) is separate and independently argues for patience. On B023 I disagree somewhat: Eriksson's worry about theory versus experiment applies, but the 1995 gate proposal directly created a concrete experimental programme, which I think is more than a method contribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to distinguish the lattice-clock achievement from the earlier frequency-comb and trapped-ion prizes, and how to word the citation to reflect that.
How much weight to give the fact that the redefinition of the second has not yet taken place.
Whether Sr and Yb lattice contributions outside the supplied pair would be seen as a defect in the Katori and Ye attribution.
For B034, whether Blais or Girvin should be omitted, and whether the committee wishes to honour superconducting circuits so soon after 2025.
statement.conflict_note: I rank circuit QED (B034) first in my opening ballot and work in the same area: I am at Chalmers and direct WACQT, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are documented connections, as is my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum. Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from the decisive discussion of B034 if it became a serious contender. No specific conflict with B004 or B023 is apparent from the provided profile.
